We’re looking for curious developers, designers, researchers, space enthusiasts, and strong communicators who want to collaborate, experiment, and build something impactful.
summary:
ORBIT is a crew health self-monitoring prototype designed for the realities of long-duration space missions. It gives crew members a simple way to record daily observations—such as sleep, energy, stress, symptoms, and optional measurements—and review how those observations change over time. They can add follow-up entries, set personal reminders, and prepare a summary to support a conversation through the mission’s established medical process.

The project connects these everyday check-ins to public NASA human spaceflight research, including on-demand metadata from the Open Science Data Repository. It also makes an important distinction: research datasets are not live astronaut health feeds, and ORBIT does not diagnose or replace medical care.

On long missions, small changes may be harder to notice or communicate. ORBIT aims to make those changes easier for an astronaut to track and discuss, using a practical, privacy-conscious interface that works locally in the browser.
details:
ORBIT is a browser-based prototype that helps crew members keep track of self-reported health observations during long-duration missions. A crew member can enter a daily check-in covering sleep, energy, focus, stress, symptoms, optional measurements, and countermeasure activities. They can add a follow-up later the same day, review personal trends, set reminders, and prepare or export a summary for discussion through the mission’s established medical process. Records stay in the current browser rather than being sent to a server.

The project also includes a research library linking NASA human spaceflight resources and selected Open Science Data Repository studies. Its on-demand metadata lookup connects to NASA’s public OSDR API. These records provide research context; they are not live astronaut telemetry, and ORBIT does not use them to diagnose an individual.

The intended benefit is to make changes easier for a crew member to notice, record, and communicate while far from routine terrestrial care. ORBIT’s creative focus is on showing personal patterns without turning them into an unexplained health score. The team considered usability during a demanding mission, privacy, offline access, clarity about fictional demo data, and the difference between self-reported observations and clinical measurements.

The prototype was developed with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and a small Python local server. It uses browser storage and a service worker; no special hardware or external JavaScript libraries are required. It is an independent concept, not a medical device or NASA-endorsed product.
